patient.name: Gloria Mensah
patient.complaint: Sudden right thigh pain after a minor stumble at home; cannot weight-bear
background: Breast cancer 8 years ago: mastectomy, then 5 years of letrozole
Aching right thigh for 3 months, worse at night
Retired nurse from Peckham; lives alone

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely cause' with a fracture after trivial trauma: known cancer and lytic lesions (metastasis), anaemia with high calcium (myeloma), or an osteoporotic pattern (wrist, vertebra, hip).

points: Gloria, 72, caught her foot on a rug and **stumbled**, not fell.
Felt a **crack** in her right thigh; cannot stand.
Thigh has **ached for 3 months**, worse at night.

steps.lead: A femur should not break from a stumble. Gloria's bone was **weakened by underlying pathology**, most likely a breast cancer metastasis.

steps.q: What in Gloria's story most suggests a pathological fracture?
o: Minor trauma after months of night pain
steps.r: **Disproportionately minor trauma** plus preceding **night pain** in a patient with previous cancer points to bone weakened by tumour.

steps.lead: Gloria fits two patterns: **older adult with known cancer** (suspect malignancy) and **postmenopausal** woman. Her night pain points to metastatic bone disease.
Gloria's **breast** primary is one of the five cancers that most often spread to bone.

steps.title: Cancers that spread to bone
steps.caption: Older patient, fracture after trivial trauma, any of these in the history: think metastasis.

steps.lead: Gloria's X-ray will show a **lytic** metastasis. In a teenager, onion-skin reaction means Ewing's; a soap bubble means giant cell tumour.

head: Pattern
Think of
rows: Lytic lesion, older adult, known cancer
Multiple punched-out lytic lesions, anaemia, high calcium
'**Soap bubble**' lytic lesion near a joint
Vertebral wedge, Colles' wrist, neck of femur

steps.lead: Gloria is at risk of **recurrent fractures**, **hypercalcaemia of malignancy** and, if the spine is involved, **spinal cord compression**.

steps.text: Known bone metastases plus **back pain** and new **leg weakness** or **urinary retention** is metastatic **spinal cord compression** until proven otherwise: urgent whole-spine MRI.

points: Right femur X-ray: **lytic lesion** in the proximal shaft.
A transverse fracture runs **through the abnormal bone**.

steps.lead: Gloria's X-ray shows the fracture **through abnormal bone**; now bloods for **calcium, ALP** and a **myeloma screen**.

steps.title: Gloria's bloods
steps.text: High calcium and ALP fit lytic metastases; the negative myeloma screen makes myeloma unlikely.

visual.title: Gloria's adjusted calcium

visual.caption: Bone destruction releases calcium: hypercalcaemia of malignancy is a complication to treat.

steps.text: In **myeloma** the lesions are purely lytic and osteoblasts are suppressed, so **ALP is usually normal**. A high ALP fits metastases like Gloria's.

steps.q: Which investigation best shows the extent of Gloria's disease?
o: Staging CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis
steps.r: **CT** (or MRI) assesses the **extent** of disease; DEXA measures bone density, not metastases.

steps.lead: Gloria's staging **CT** shows two small lytic spinal deposits and no visceral disease; **MRI** would detail marrow and cord involvement.
Bone taken during Gloria's femoral fixation is sent for **biopsy**: the gold standard that confirms the cause.

steps.title: Investigating a suspected pathological fracture
nodes: CT or MRI: extent of disease

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?': fixation for weight-bearing bones, a sling for a closed humeral shaft fracture, then treat the cause (radiotherapy, bisphosphonate, chemotherapy) and prevent further fractures.

points: Right leg in a temporary splint.

steps.q: Gloria's femur has broken through a metastasis. Which is the most appropriate management?
steps.r: A fracture in a **weight-bearing bone** needs **orthopaedic stabilisation**; radiotherapy and bisphosphonates come afterwards.

steps.lead: Gloria's **femur** is weight-bearing, so she goes to theatre for **orthopaedic stabilisation** (an intramedullary nail).
Gloria needs **fixation** and stepwise analgesia from **paracetamol to opioids**. A closed humeral shaft fracture would just need a **sling**.

points: Oncology plan: radiotherapy to the femur.

steps.lead: Gloria gets **radiotherapy** for the metastasis and IV **zoledronic acid** to strengthen bone. Myeloma would mean **chemotherapy**; osteoporosis, an oral bisphosphonate.

visual.title: Gloria's calcium after zoledronic acid
visual.caption: Zoledronic acid switches off osteoclasts and brings calcium back into range.

visual.title: eGFR and oral bisphosphonate
visual.label: Gloria 64
visual.caption: Alendronic acid needs eGFR above 35. If bisphosphonates are contraindicated altogether, use denosumab.

steps.title: Long-term fracture prevention
nodes: Oral not possible → IV zoledronic acid

steps.text: Do not treat a pathological fracture as a simple fracture. Fixing the bone without finding and treating the **cause** leads to **recurrent fracture**.

steps.lead: Gloria's zoledronic acid, and the alendronate or denosumab choices for osteoporosis, follow **NICE bisphosphonate and denosumab guidance**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why breast metastases are lytic and prostate ones sclerotic, why osteoporosis weakens bone, and how bisphosphonates and denosumab work.

steps.lead: Gloria's femur was hollowed out by **tumour infiltration**, so a force that a normal femur shrugs off broke it.

steps.r: Breast metastases **stimulate osteoclasts**, destroying bone. Prostate metastases stimulate osteoblasts and look sclerotic.

steps.lead: Gloria's **breast** deposits are **osteolytic**; a man with **prostate** cancer would have dense **osteoblastic** lesions.

steps.title: The vicious cycle of lytic metastasis

steps.lead: Gloria is also **postmenopausal**: **oestrogen deficiency** tips remodelling towards osteoclastic resorption, lowering bone density everywhere.
Gloria's **zoledronic acid** is taken up by osteoclasts and triggers their **apoptosis**. **Denosumab** blocks **RANKL** instead, regardless of kidney function.

steps.text: **Osteomalacia** weakens bone differently: osteoid is laid down but **not mineralised**, so calcium is low and urinary calcium is low.

o: A fracture in bone weakened by underlying disease
A fracture that has failed to unite
A stress fracture in an athlete
mcq.r: A fracture in bone **weakened by underlying pathology**, from disproportionately minor trauma.

mcq.r: **Onion-skin** lamellated periosteal reaction; soap bubble is giant cell tumour.

mcq.r: **Colles'** (wrist), vertebral wedge and neck of femur fractures are osteoporotic patterns.

mcq.r: **Biopsy of the lesion** confirms the cause.
**Calcium, ALP and a myeloma screen**, alongside the X-ray.

What eGFR is needed for alendronic acid?
What is the mechanism of denosumab?
mcq.r: **Anti-RANKL monoclonal antibody**, reducing resorption independent of renal function.

Giant cell tumour: soap bubble appearance

prompts.q: Why are some bone metastases lytic and others sclerotic, and why does osteoporosis increase fracture risk?

points.p: Osteolytic (e.g. breast): stimulate osteoclasts, bone destruction
Osteoblastic (e.g. prostate): stimulate new bone formation
Osteoporosis: resorption exceeds formation, low BMD
points.why: Accelerated by oestrogen deficiency or glucocorticoids.

prompts.q: How do bisphosphonates and denosumab work?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two routes to fewer osteoclasts.

glossary.Pathological fracture: A fracture through bone weakened by disease, caused by trauma that would not break normal bone.
glossary.Fragility fracture: A fracture from a fall from standing height or less, typically due to osteoporosis.
glossary.Metastasis: Cancer that has spread from its original site to another organ, such as bone.
glossary.Lytic lesion: An area where bone has been destroyed, appearing as a dark hole on X-ray.
glossary.Sclerotic lesion: An area of abnormally dense new bone, appearing whiter on X-ray.
glossary.Osteolytic: Causing bone destruction, as in breast cancer metastases.
glossary.Osteoblastic: Causing new bone formation, as in prostate cancer metastases.
glossary.Multiple myeloma: A cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow causing lytic lesions, anaemia, high calcium and kidney damage.
glossary.Myeloma screen: Tests for myeloma: serum protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains and urine Bence Jones protein.
glossary.Paraprotein: An abnormal antibody made by a single clone of plasma cells, seen in myeloma.
glossary.Osteoporosis: Low bone mass and weakened bone structure, increasing fracture risk.
glossary.Osteomalacia: Soft bones from defective mineralisation, usually due to vitamin D deficiency.
glossary.BMD: Bone mineral density, measured by DEXA scan.
glossary.DEXA: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, a scan measuring bone mineral density.
glossary.ALP: Alkaline phosphatase, an enzyme raised when bone turnover is high.
glossary.Adjusted calcium: Serum calcium corrected for the albumin level.
glossary.Hypercalcaemia of malignancy: High calcium from cancer, through bone destruction or PTHrP release.
glossary.Spinal cord compression: Pressure on the spinal cord, here from vertebral metastases, causing back pain, weakness and sphincter loss.
glossary.Ewing's sarcoma: A malignant bone tumour of children and young adults, with an onion-skin periosteal reaction.
glossary.Onion-skin: Layered periosteal new bone on X-ray, typical of Ewing's sarcoma.
glossary.Giant cell tumour: A usually benign but locally aggressive bone tumour near joints, with a soap bubble X-ray look.
glossary.Soap bubble: A multi-chambered lytic X-ray appearance, typical of giant cell tumour.
glossary.Periosteal reaction: New bone formed by the periosteum in response to tumour, infection or injury.
glossary.Vertebral wedge fracture: Collapse of the front of a vertebral body, typical of osteoporosis.
glossary.Colles' fracture: A distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement after a fall on an outstretched hand.
glossary.Intramedullary nail: A metal rod inserted down the marrow cavity of a long bone to fix a fracture.
glossary.Bisphosphonates: Drugs that bind bone mineral and kill osteoclasts, reducing bone resorption.
glossary.Alendronic acid: An oral weekly bisphosphonate for osteoporosis; requires eGFR above 35.
glossary.Zoledronic acid: An IV bisphosphonate used for bone metastases, myeloma and osteoporosis.
glossary.Denosumab: A monoclonal antibody against RANKL, given every 6 months, that reduces bone resorption.
glossary.RANKL: A signal from osteoblasts that activates osteoclasts to resorb bone.
glossary.Osteoclast: A bone cell that breaks down bone.
glossary.Osteoblast: A bone cell that builds new bone.
glossary.Hydroxyapatite: The calcium phosphate mineral that makes bone hard.
glossary.Osteoid: The unmineralised protein matrix of bone, laid down by osteoblasts.
glossary.PTHrP: Parathyroid hormone-related protein, released by some cancers, which raises calcium and drives bone resorption.
glossary.Teriparatide: A PTH analogue that builds bone; avoided in skeletal malignancy.
glossary.Radiotherapy: Treatment with ionising radiation to kill cancer cells, used for painful bone metastases.

technique.stem: A 70 year old woman has severe right thigh pain after tripping on a step. She could not get up. She has had a dull ache in the thigh, worse at night, for 2 months. She had breast cancer 6 years ago. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg. X-ray shows a femoral shaft fracture through an area of bone destruction.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: what kind of fracture is this?

clues: through an area of bone destruction
steps.x: Minor trauma, preceding night pain, previous breast cancer, lytic lesion, raised calcium and ALP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pathological fracture through a breast metastasis**.

elim: Osteoporosis does not cause a lytic lesion or night pain before the fracture.
Osteomalacia gives low calcium, not high.
Osteosarcoma is a primary tumour of adolescents.
Paget's gives thickened bone, not focal destruction with a cancer history.

steps.x: **E. Pathological fracture through a metastasis.** Rule: old cancer + trivial trauma + lytic lesion = metastasis.

technique.stem: A 68 year old man has a fracture of the left humerus after lifting a shopping bag. X-ray shows a lytic lesion at the fracture site. He has a history of renal cell carcinoma treated 4 years ago. His calcium, ALP and myeloma screen have been sent. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess the extent of disease?
o: Staging CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis

steps.x: It asks for extent, so this is the second-line step after X-ray and bloods.
Pathological fracture from a likely kidney metastasis; first-line done.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT** (or MRI) to stage.

elim: DEXA measures bone density, not metastases.
Repeating the X-ray adds nothing about spread.
ALP is already part of first-line bloods.
Ultrasound cannot stage bone disease.

steps.x: **D. Staging CT.** Rule: X-ray and bloods first, CT or MRI for extent, biopsy to confirm.

technique.stem: A 66 year old woman has had surgical fixation of a pathological femoral fracture caused by a breast cancer metastasis. She is to have radiotherapy to the femur. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate bone-strengthening treatment?

steps.x: Long-term bone treatment in metastatic disease.
Bone metastases, a raised calcium and good kidney function.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IV bisphosphonate: **zoledronic acid**.

elim: Calcitonin is not a standard bone-strengthening treatment.
Calcium and vitamin D alone are inadequate, and she is hypercalcaemic.
HRT is contraindicated after breast cancer.
Teriparatide is avoided in skeletal malignancy.

steps.x: **E. Zoledronic acid.** Rule: bone metastases = radiotherapy + bisphosphonate.

technique.stem: A 74 year old woman with osteoporosis and a previous wrist fracture is started on weekly oral alendronic acid. She asks how the tablet will make her bones stronger.
technique.q: Which is the mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Binds hydroxyapatite and induces osteoclast apoptosis
Stimulates osteoblasts via the PTH receptor

steps.x: A mechanism question on a named bisphosphonate.
Alendronic acid is a **bisphosphonate**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Binds **hydroxyapatite**, is ingested by osteoclasts and induces their **apoptosis**.

elim: Blocking RANKL is denosumab.
Increasing calcium absorption is vitamin D (calcitriol).
Xanthine oxidase inhibition is allopurinol.
PTH receptor stimulation is teriparatide.

steps.x: **A. Binds hydroxyapatite, osteoclast apoptosis.** Rule: bisphosphonate = osteoclast death; denosumab = anti-RANKL.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman falls onto her outstretched right hand from standing height. Her wrist is painful and has a 'dinner fork' deformity. She is postmenopausal and has taken prednisolone for 3 years for polymyalgia rheumatica. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 142/80 mmHg. X-ray shows a distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A dorsally displaced distal radius fracture after a fall on an outstretched hand in a postmenopausal woman on steroids is an osteoporotic Colles' fracture. Smith's is volar displacement.

steps.x: Name the fracture pattern.

clues: falls onto her outstretched right hand
steps.x: Low-impact fall, osteoporosis risk factors, dorsal displacement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Osteoporotic **Colles' fracture**.

elim: Barton's is an intra-articular rim fracture with carpal dislocation.
Galeazzi is radial shaft fracture with distal radioulnar dislocation.
Scaphoid gives snuffbox tenderness, no dinner fork.
Smith's fracture is volar (palmar) displacement.

steps.x: **B. Colles' fracture.** Rule: osteoporotic wrist + dorsal displacement = Colles'.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man has back pain after lifting a box. He has felt tired for 3 months and has had recurrent chest infections. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. X-ray shows a vertebral compression fracture and multiple punched-out lytic lesions in the skull.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his fracture?
practice.e: Lytic lesions with anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, infections and a normal ALP point to multiple myeloma. Prostate metastases are sclerotic with a raised ALP.

steps.x: The cause of a pathological fracture.

clues: punched-out lytic lesions in the skull
steps.x: CRAB: high calcium, renal impairment, anaemia, bone lesions; infections; normal ALP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Multiple myeloma**.

elim: Prostate metastases are sclerotic with a raised ALP.
Osteomalacia gives low calcium and a high ALP.
Osteoporosis does not cause lytic lesions or anaemia.
Paget's has a very high ALP and normal calcium.

steps.x: **B. Multiple myeloma.** Rule: lytic lesions + CRAB + normal ALP = myeloma.

practice.stem: A 15 year old boy has a 2 month history of pain and swelling in his left thigh, worse at night, with fevers and fatigue. He recently fractured the femur after a minor tackle at football. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. X-ray shows a lytic lesion of the femoral diaphysis with a lamellated periosteal reaction.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A teenager with night pain, fever, a pathological fracture and a lytic lesion with lamellated 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction has Ewing's sarcoma. Giant cell tumour gives a soap bubble.

steps.x: Diagnosis of the lesion causing a pathological fracture in a teenager.
Young, night pain, systemic symptoms, minor trauma, onion-skin reaction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ewing's sarcoma**.

elim: Giant cell tumour is a soap bubble lesion near the knee in young adults.
Osteoid osteoma is a small sclerotic nidus with night pain relieved by NSAIDs.
Osteomyelitis is more acute; the onion-skin pattern points to tumour.
A simple bone cyst is well-defined and causes no fever.

steps.x: **A. Ewing's sarcoma.** Rule: onion-skin = Ewing's; soap bubble = giant cell tumour.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has a pathological fracture of the right femur through a lytic lesion. He has had intermittent painless visible haematuria and weight loss for 4 months. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 152/90 mmHg. There is a firm mass in the right flank.
practice.q: Which is the most likely site of the primary tumour?
practice.e: Haematuria, a flank mass and polycythaemia suggest renal cell carcinoma, one of the five classic primaries that spread to bone.

steps.x: Which primary caused the bone metastasis?

clues: firm mass in the right flank
steps.x: Haematuria plus flank mass, and a raised haemoglobin from erythropoietin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Kidney** (renal cell carcinoma).

elim: Bladder cancer causes haematuria but not a flank mass, and rarely bone metastases.
Colon cancer seldom spreads to bone.
Oesophageal cancer gives dysphagia.
Pancreatic cancer gives jaundice and weight loss, rarely bone deposits.

steps.x: **C. Kidney.** Rule: breast, prostate, thyroid, kidney, lung go to bone.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman who rarely leaves the house has a fracture of the left femoral neck after a minor fall. She has had aching bones and difficulty climbing stairs for a year. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her fracture?
practice.e: Low calcium, low phosphate, raised ALP, low vitamin D and low urinary calcium with bone pain and proximal weakness is osteomalacia. Osteoporosis has normal bloods.

steps.x: The bone disease behind the fracture; use the biochemistry.
No sunlight, bone pain, proximal myopathy; calcium, phosphate and urinary calcium low, ALP high.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Osteomalacia** from vitamin D deficiency.

elim: Hyperparathyroidism raises calcium.
Osteoporosis has normal calcium, phosphate and ALP.
Paget's has a high ALP but normal calcium and phosphate.
Renal osteodystrophy needs CKD with a high phosphate.

steps.x: **B. Osteomalacia.** Rule: low calcium + low urinary calcium + high ALP = osteomalacia.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man with prostate cancer and known spinal metastases has 2 days of worsening back pain and weakness in both legs. He has not passed urine for 10 hours. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 146/86 mmHg. There is reduced power in both legs and a sensory level at T10.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: Back pain, bilateral leg weakness, a sensory level and urinary retention in a man with spinal metastases is metastatic spinal cord compression, an emergency needing whole-spine MRI.

steps.x: Which complication of bone metastases?
Cord signs at a level with bladder involvement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Metastatic spinal cord compression**.

elim: Brain metastases do not give a sensory level.
Hypercalcaemia gives confusion, thirst, constipation, not a sensory level.
Paraneoplastic syndromes do not cause a sudden sensory level.
No fever or infection risk is given.

steps.x: **C. Metastatic spinal cord compression.** Rule: bone mets + leg weakness + retention = MSCC.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man has no history of cancer. He has a lytic lesion in the proximal humerus with a fracture through it after minor trauma. Myeloma screen is negative and CT shows no other lesions or primary tumour. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: Biopsy of the lesion is the gold standard to confirm the cause of a pathological fracture, especially with no known primary.

steps.x: 'Confirm' means the gold standard.

clues: no other lesions or primary tumour
steps.x: Solitary lytic lesion, cause unknown.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Biopsy** of the lesion.

elim: A bone scan shows spread, not a tissue diagnosis.
PET-CT localises disease but does not confirm histology.
Waiting delays a possible cancer diagnosis.
PSA suggests prostate cancer but cannot confirm what the bone lesion is.

steps.x: **A. Biopsy of the lesion.** Rule: biopsy confirms; imaging stages.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman has a fracture of the left femoral shaft after stumbling at home. X-ray shows the fracture runs through a lytic lesion. She has no known cancer. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 140/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Alongside the X-ray, first-line investigations are calcium, ALP and a myeloma screen. Imaging for extent and biopsy follow.

steps.x: Initial test after the X-ray.
Pathological fracture, cause unknown: myeloma and metastasis both possible.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Calcium, ALP and a myeloma screen**.

elim: Biopsy confirms the cause but is not the first step.
DEXA measures density, not a lytic lesion.
Whole-spine MRI is for suspected cord compression or extent later.
PET-CT is not first-line.

steps.x: **B. Calcium, ALP and myeloma screen.** Rule: X-ray + bloods first.

practice.stem: A 69 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer has a fracture of the right femoral shaft through a lytic lesion after a minor fall. She has had morphine for pain. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management of the fracture?
o: Surgical fixation with an intramedullary nail
practice.e: A pathological fracture of a weight-bearing bone needs orthopaedic stabilisation. Radiotherapy and bisphosphonates treat the cause but do not stabilise the fracture.

steps.x: Management of the fracture itself.
Weight-bearing long bone through a metastasis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Orthopaedic stabilisation**.

elim: A cast cannot stabilise a femoral shaft fracture.
Prolonged bed rest causes harm and does not heal pathological bone.
Radiotherapy follows fixation; it does not stabilise.
Zoledronic acid strengthens bone long term, not a fracture now.

steps.x: **D. Surgical fixation.** Rule: weight-bearing bone = stabilise.

practice.stem: An 81 year old woman with osteoporosis falls at home and has pain in her left upper arm. X-ray shows a closed, minimally displaced fracture of the humeral shaft. There is no wrist drop and the skin is intact. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 144/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Uncomplicated closed humeral shaft fractures are managed conservatively with a basic sling and analgesia.

steps.x: Management of an osteoporotic humeral shaft fracture.
Uncomplicated: closed, no radial nerve palsy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Basic sling**.

elim: External fixators are for open or contaminated fractures.
Nailing is for unstable or failed conservative cases.
ORIF is for complicated or displaced fractures.
Hemiarthroplasty is for complex proximal humeral fractures.

steps.x: **A. Basic sling.** Rule: closed uncomplicated humeral shaft = sling.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman has had an osteoporotic vertebral fracture. She has an oesophageal stricture and cannot take oral bisphosphonates. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment to prevent further fractures?
practice.e: When oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated, IV zoledronic acid is used. Denosumab is for when bisphosphonates are contraindicated altogether, for example in severe renal impairment.

steps.x: Fracture prevention when oral treatment is not possible.
Oral route out; kidneys fine (eGFR 66).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IV bisphosphonate: **zoledronic acid**.

elim: Alendronic acid is oral, contraindicated by the stricture.
Calcitriol alone does not prevent osteoporotic fractures.
Denosumab is for when all bisphosphonates are contraindicated.
Raloxifene is not the next step here.

steps.x: **E. Zoledronic acid.** Rule: oral out = IV zoledronic acid; all bisphosphonates out = denosumab.

practice.stem: A 64 year old woman with breast cancer has a pathological fracture of the left humerus. X-ray shows several areas of bone destruction. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her bone lesions?
practice.e: Breast metastases are osteolytic: tumour stimulates osteoclast activity, causing bone destruction and hypercalcaemia. Prostate metastases stimulate osteoblasts.

steps.x: Mechanism behind lytic metastases.
Breast primary, lytic lesions, raised calcium.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Tumour-driven **osteoclast activity**.

elim: Defective mineralisation is osteomalacia.
Excess osteoblast activity is prostate (sclerotic) metastasis.
Oestrogen deficiency gives diffuse osteoporosis, not focal destruction.
Plasma cell infiltration is myeloma.

steps.x: **C. Increased osteoclast activity.** Rule: breast lytic (osteoclast), prostate sclerotic (osteoblast).
